In the same item it is defined that military policemen joining MP companies shall take with them the complete equipment and weapons. And also in the same item it says that motor vehicles and other equipment of the military platoons shall be transferred to the military police companies and registered as returned by the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you there, Mr. Biskic, since we will all have the document before you. What were the -- what was the primary motivating factor in this reorganisation that's outlined and detailed in a great amount of detail in P 07018?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Well, the information about the establishment of the military police of the Croatian Defence Council at that time, that's what led me, and they were working as platoons in the brigades and battalions in the military districts, and there were the light assault military battalions of the military police. Similarly, the system of command between the military police and the commander of the platoons in the brigades was not properly defined, and I thought that there could be a simplified system which at that time I felt would have been more efficacious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, following this document that we've just seen or the issuance of that document, were there a series of documents to lower-level units implementing that more general order?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please take a look, Mr. Biskic, at the document marked 7040, which should be the next document in the bundle. That's P 07040. Can you tell it us what this document is, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: This document -- well, in fact it's an order that I signed as assistant minister for security, and by this order I regulate the implementation of the order by the minister of defence dated the 3rd of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which is the document we just looked at; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I say here: "I hereby order to order the acting --" or, rather, the Ministry of Defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, I make him responsible for the implementation of the five points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, it would appear, sir, at the bottom of this document under your signature that this was sent to the minister of defence, Mr. Perica Jukic, and to the minister of interior, Mr. Valentin Coric; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, why this letter was addressed to Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Valentin Coric, as of the 11th of November, 1993, was the minister of the interior of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and in point 2 of this order, point 2 and 3, cooperation is defined with the police units and police administration of the military police of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and thereby I considered that this order should go to the attention of minister of the interior of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna or, rather, Mr. Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Biskic, any meetings that dealt with the subject of cooperation between the ministry of the defence -- or Ministry of Defence and the MUP that you attended with Mr. Coric in December 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Well, there were joint meetings between or in the Ministry of Defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna at which the minister of the interior was present, Mr. Valentin Coric. And at those meetings they discussed close cooperation between the military and civilian police as being necessary. And before that as well. There was a certain amount of cooperation between the military and civilian police forces, and that's why I considered that by this order we would move to a new establishment and that we should more clearly define this cooperation. And personally with the minister of the interior of HR HB, I had a meeting with the assistant minister later on towards the 17th of December, 1993, where we looked at more concrete forms of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With respect to this meeting on the 17th of December, 1993, sir, do you recall some of the topics that were discussed with respect to, as you put it, more concrete forms of cooperation?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the meeting of the 17th of November or December 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: December. I see a reference on the transcript to 17 December, 1993, that you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall some of the things that were discussed in terms of more concrete forms of cooperation between the MUP and the MOD?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: In concrete terms the Ministry of the Interior and the ministry of police of the Croatian Defence Council, well, we talked about a joint patrol service and check-points and taking over supervision by the civilian police or the Ministry of the Interior of the HR HB at the border crossings with the republic of Croatia, and also taking over security for humanitarian convoys by the civilian police or Ministry of the Interior of the HR HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, could you look at the next document in the binder in front of you, which is marked 7218, that is P 07218.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please, the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: 7218. Are you familiar with this document, Mr. Biskic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's the document I referred to a while ago which relates to the conclusions from the meeting that I held on the 17th of December with the then minister of the interior, Mr. Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you please turn to the next document in the bundle which is 7243, P 07234 -- 43, sorry. 43. P 07243. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: It is my order to the head of the military police administration, rather, the acting minister, about the implementation of the conclusions reached at the meeting of the 17th of December, 1993, with the minister of the interior, Mr. Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn now, sir, to a slightly different topic concerning military police restructuring. Do you recall a meeting held on the 14th of December, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, first of all, where this meeting was held and what the purpose of this meeting was?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, and if we are referring to the same meeting, I think it was held in Mostar with a group of officers of the military police, and the topic discussed was the new organisation and the tasks and assignments of the military police and their officers in the ensuing period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, can you elaborate upon the tasks and assignments for that period? What were you trying to accomplish with these tasks and assignments?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: You mean the restructuring of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Is that what you mean? Well, with this restructuring of the Croatian Defence Council, I wanted to ensure more -- a simpler system of control and command and more efficacious implementation of military police tasks. I also wanted to achieve firmer subordination and coordination with all the military police units by the military police administration, and I wanted to define the role of the commander of the HVO units and the military police units in their areas of responsibility, and of course to achieve better results, generally speaking, in the work of the military police during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn, sir, to the document marked 7169, P 07169.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps -- [Interpretation] Perhaps, Your Honour, before we move on, while it's still on our screens, in the previous answer by the witness on page 53 [as interpreted], it says that he wished to ensure stronger control, but the witness also said "clearer," "clearer control," clearer relationships between the HVO and the military police. So not firmer but clearer. Perhaps we could have the question repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, in your opinion was there problems with the clarity of the situation between the military police units and other HVO units?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I think that in the command and control system there were things that weren't clear enough, especially the platoons of the military police attached to the brigades, and this could be seen from the reports by the acting person and his reports sent into the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you mean by, "in the command and control system things were clear enough"? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I think that clearer -- what I meant by "clearer" was the regulations on the work of the Croatian Defence Council signed, as far as I can remember, in April 1992. It referred to the place and role of the chief of the military police in issuing orders to the military police units and the relationship of the brigade commander of the military district vis-a-vis the military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can help clarify the situation or an explanation. Was it the situation that things were simply confusing, or was it the situation that with respect to the military police there was a complete breakdown of command and control, or was it something else or something in between?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think there was a breakdown in control and command, but there was lack of understanding of the system of control and command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] The witness has already given the answer, but I would like to say what I intended to say in the first place. I think that the term used by the Prosecutor is a very general one, so when we speak of specific and concrete matters, a concrete question would be in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, could you not have said it in the cross-examination? Why did you see fit to intervene at this point? Right. For clarification purposes. Continue, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's turn then, sir, to this document 7169 that you have before you, which is P 07169. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with it. I saw it when I talked to the Prosecutor -- or, rather, the representatives of the OTP in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, this purports to be minutes of that meeting on the 14th of December, 1993, in Mostar. Can you take a look at this document and give us your views as to whether this accurately reflects what occurred at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: The minutes were kept by the military police administration. I can just guess, hazard a guess and says what is written down here is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For purposes of clarification, sir, did you attend this meeting on the 14th of December, 1993, in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present for part of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall which part of the meeting you were present for?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: The first part of the meeting. And it began at 1200 hours, then somewhere after 1400 hours I believe I left. But I can't say when that was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was the primary purpose of this meeting which seems to have had a large number of attendees? What was the primary reason for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: The prime reason for the meeting was for me to get to know the officers of the military police, to meet them in this restructuring. I wanted to introduce myself. I wanted them to hear me, and I wanted to answer some of their questions and queries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, what the general mood or atmosphere was with respect to this reorganisation of the HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: What I received, the feedback and information I received and what I could feel at the meeting was that the atmosphere was normal, because before that there was restructuring of the military police from its inception until my arrival.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, looking at this document, one is surprised to see here that you introduce yourselves, and you're introducing your collaborators, and they all come from the Republic of Croatia. The names are Boro Gambiraza, there is Captain Cvitanovic, et cetera. Now, a question in that regard. Why was the Republic of Croatia so much present in -- at a function that only seemed to concern the HVO? Why did you see the need to surround yourself with collaborators coming from the Republic of Croatia? Does it mean that at the level of Herzegovina, or Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was nobody capable of filling those posts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the answer to your question, Mr. President, is something that this document does. It speaks for itself because next to me there were two officers from the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, and all the rest at this meeting and all the people who worked to implement the new organisation both of the military police of the HVO and the security and information service were and remain officers or, rather, members of the Croatian Defence Council. So my answer is that at the time and before me and after me there were capable officers of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but one could gain the impression, looking at this from the outside, that there is -- that your placing this under control, your control. What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said at the beginning that I came to help out in the -- to help out in the situation that was held by the HVO, and I said I came to assist. Not pursuant to an order, but I considered that since I was born on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina it was my honour and pleasure and privilege to help out. It was no control. I was not subordinate to anyone, General Roso, minister Soljic, later on. And while I was down there, I really felt like a member of the HVO. And together with the HVO officers, I took part in the reorganisation and restructuring of the military police and the security and information service and the adjustment of the HVO which followed at the beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt you. You -- if I am not mistaken, you had a sentence here which says that -- that, "I was not subordinate to anyone. General Roso, minister -- minister --" I don't -- I cannot read that, and later on. Now, do you say you have not been subordinated to anybody, meaning not subordinated to the minister himself, or probably it is a question of translation? So were you subordinate as assistant minister to the minister, or you were not? That is my question. And as far as the translation is concerned, of course, we have to look into it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me repeat. I said the following: I was not subordinate to anyone in the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. At the point in time when I arrived in the territory of the Croatian Defence Council, during November I was at a time subordinate to General Roso. He was my superior. And later on I was subordinated to the minister of defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, who was Mr. Jukic. And later on once again to the minister, Vladimir Soljic. So once again let me repeat. I was in the system of command and control of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and I was subordinated later on as assistant minister to Minister Jukic or, rather, Minister Soljic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much for the clarification, and it was an issue of the translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for clarification purposes, the gentleman during his six-day interview, six or seven, I believe it's six days, at one point he does indicate that he was seconded, that was the term that was used and was acknowledged by the Office of the Prosecution. Seconded. In other words, he was seconded from the Republic of Croatia to -- to the HVO. So perhaps a line of question, and that may assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And a final question from me. So this document speaks of how you intervened, and once you introduced your collaborators, you said that the object of this meeting was to create a military police that was honourable. Now, I'm wondering about the sense and meaning of your words there. Does that mean that the military police before that was not an honourable one? What did you want to say by using that term? You can look at the text of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said at the beginning that I assumed that they conveyed my words as I said them. However, I say with full responsibility here before the Court, before the Trial Chamber and everybody in the courtroom here, that I never said that they were unhonourable, the military policemen of the Croatian Defence Council were not honourable, and the military police of the HVO. And I do believe that my words were not conveyed as I uttered them in this sentence, because had I used that word, there would certainly would have been reactions from the people at the meeting, because there were certainly representatives and people who had worked in the military police before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again for clarification purposes, during the lengthy interview the gentleman did point out that the minutes of the meetings were not accurately recorded. And I mention this because I think in fairness to the gentleman this should be brought out. If he's going to be asked about a specific section on the minutes of the meeting, in fairness to the gentleman, they should also point out where he gave full and fair and complete explanations as to what he believed he said or others said and what the minutes may not accurately reflect what was said, because he indicated that the minutes were not -- did not -- were not verbatim. This was not a recorded or videotaped meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I just note for the transcript quite simply that this document indicates that the meeting ended at 1555 hours and that there were two persons who signed this document jointly, Mr. Radoslav Lavric and Mr. Renate Peric. And it says minutes taken by Renate Peric. So Renate Peric was the editor of the document. Continue, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Biskic, let me ask you some more questions on this issue of reporting. During the time period that you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to whom did you report?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I shall repeat for the second time today. I reported to General Roso at first, then to the Minister Jukic, and as of 25 February, to Minister Vladimir Soljic. I'm talking about the ministers in the Ministry of Defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time period, sir, that you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you make any reports to any authorities in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't duty-bound to report to anybody, and I didn't. In that position, I did not report to anybody. I did send two letters to the then minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Gojko Susak, but not as my superior but as a person who did have a certain influence on the officers in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna because he hailed from Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's where he was born. And he came to the territory under the control of the Croatian Defence Council quite often. In order to make myself clear, I sent him two reports to inform him about the situation and to ask him to use his influence in order to speed up certain processes in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Biskic, I'm going to ask you some questions about these two documents, but before this goes off the screen, if you could please look at lines 4 and 5 of page 57 on the screen in front of you where you said that you reported to General Roso, then Minister Jukic, and as of 25 February, to Minister Vladimir Soljic. And I'm going to ask you if that's the correct name, Vladimir Soljic.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Soljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you spell that, please? Is that spelled correctly?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Vladimir Soljic, Mr. Vladimir Soljic who took over the duty as the minister of defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. And I believe that this was sometime in February, and I had come from Croatia where I was on holiday because of the illness of my wife, and on the 25th of February I got introduced to the new minister. I believe that the name is Soljic, Soljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you told us, and this is on lines 15 and 16 of page 57, that Mr. Susak came to the territory under the Croatian Defence Council quite often. Do you recall, sir, approximately how many occasions in Susak came to Bosnia and Herzegovina or the territory under the control of the HVO during the time period you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I believe some four or five times he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what time period, if you can be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: November December 1993, and I believe in early January of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you personally attend any of the meetings that Mr. Susak was present at in November or December 1993, or January 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes. When he arrived, we had some meetings which were not official, but meetings during which we discussed the situation in the territory of the Croatian Defence Council, i.e., in the zone of responsibility of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were -- you've told us "We had some meetings which were not official." Were there any meetings which were official?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: No. What I was saying is that these were not meetings at which Mr. Susak appeared as the Minister of Defence of the republic of Croatia. At least this is not how I perceived him. These were meetings during which he expressed interest in the situation of the Croatian Defence Council, about problems, and how he as an individual, as a person, could be of any assistance in all that. I don't know whether there were any other meetings. I am not privy to that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us other than yourself and Mr. Susak who was present at any of these meetings that you've told us about? Again in the period November 1993 through January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were the leaders of the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff. I believe that at one or two meetings there was also late Mr. Boban, the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. At one of those meetings there was also Mr. Valentin Coric as the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, sir, the leaders of the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff, the leaders of the Ministry of Defence and Main Staff of what state or country?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: When I said that he went there, of course I meant the Ministry of Defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Minister Jukic and Roso, and assistant -- assistant ministers and some of the officers of the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council. This is who I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I am still talking about these meetings. You said that the meeting ended at 17.58 and that you left about 15.55 because you had another meeting in Posusje. Before that meeting and I'm talking about another meeting that was there Mr. Marinko Maric, he started talking about the reinforcement of the front lines, and he was going to tell you about the problem, and he said that since the focus of attention has been moved the work cannot be continued by the detainees. And you told us that this decision had come from the president of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna and that you yourself were -- did not want to be detained as the war criminal, like Milosevic and Izetbegovic. Do you remember that intervention about that topic that was tackled, about the front lines, about the work of the detainees? Why did you raise the issue of war criminals within that context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that at that meeting somebody raised a similar issue indeed, and the name of Marinko Maric does not mean anything to me as I sit here. My answer was probably along the lines of what has been recorded in here. Before that, before this meeting, I believe that sometime around the 10th of December the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Boban, issued a decision on the dismantling of collection centres and the implementation of that decision lasted between sometime around 11th of December and the end of December. I believe that at the end of December the decision had been fully implemented, and I believe that the person who raised that issue probably was privy to some information about detainees being taken to the front line where they had to refortify the front line positions. My answer was very clear about those working on the front line. Likewise, if I mention, which I probably did, war criminals by their names, since we were aware of the fact that the Muslim armed forces and the armed forces of Serbia in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina also used detained Croatians to work on the front lines, during that particular meeting I also had information that detainees were taken by certain members of the Croatian Defence Council to the war operation zones. And when I learnt about that, I proposed, as early as November 1993, and I asked the chief of the General Staff to issue an order on the ban of taking prisoners and detainees from the collection centres. And on return of those who had been taken away from the collection centres for one or the other reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this answer. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, can you please turn to the document marked 7064 in the binder. That's P 07064. Are you familiar with this document, Mr. Biskic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that document is, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: This is a report which I sent to Mr. Gojko Susak. The date is 7 December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, a few moments ago, sir, you told us that you sent two reports to Mr. Susak. I take it then this is one of those two documents.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why did you send this document to Mr. Susak?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I assume that I sent it to him after I received certain information about problems in the collection centres. Also, I knew that the international community put pressure on the Republic of Croatia with regard to the situation in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Also, I thought that dealing with these issues could be accelerated if the Republic of Croatia were to get involved as well as the international organisations, and in that sense I sent this letter. Obviously, before that I informed about the information I had Mr. Jukic and the Chief of General Staff, and I also put forward some proposal for dealing with the situation that apparently prevailed in the collection centres. In November 1993, these individuals took certain measures in order to deal with the problems that prevailed in the collection centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, Mr. Biskic, and ask you about the first paragraph of this document, P 07064. There's a reference, or you write: "I immediately observed irregularities with regard to prisoner of war shelters and collection centres." Can you elaborate upon that, what you mean by irregularities with regard to prisoner of war shelters and collection centres?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: As we were preparing for the operation that was to take place in Uskoplje, or Gornji Vakuf, as you will, the chief of the SIS administration in Mostar, I received initial information about some of the war prisoners who had escaped and crossed the front line. I was also informed at the time that there were certain problems in the collection centres, and one of the problems was that the category of individuals was not clear and that there was no clear authority in terms of providing for the security of these collection centres. Also, I learnt that there was no clear procedure for prisoners of war entering those accommodation facilities and collection centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you mean, sir, by "no clear procedure for prisoners of war entering those accommodation and collection centres"? What do you mean by "no clear procedure"?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: According to the information that I received from the chief of the military police administration of the Croatian Defence Council and the Security Information Services, I thought that it was not clear how detainees entered the accommodation centres and collection centres so that the isolated persons were in a way accessible to members of the Croatian Defence Council, and these people took those prisoners to work. In order to get a clearer picture on the collection centres, on the 17th November, 1993, I issued an order asking for a report from the acting chief of the security services. We discussed his report previously. And based on that report, I proposed certain measures to the minister, Minister Jukic, which he accepted, and issued orders to the effect of regulating the visits of medical officers in the course of the month of November, 1993, and to the effect of improving the conditions of life and stay of prisoners in the collection centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about the second paragraph of this document P 07064. In the first phrase of the second paragraph you write: "There have been organisational omissions in RZ shelters and collection centres ..." What do you mean, sir, by "organisational omissions"?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: At the time when I wrote this, I implied that in the same area and under the authority of the same ministry, you couldn't have prisoners of war. You couldn't have persons who had been taken into custody for rebellion, and you couldn't have civilians who had been sent to the collection centres for safety reasons. You couldn't have all of these there at the same time under the authority of the same ministry. This is what I meant when I said "organisational omissions."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Could you please now turn to the next document in the binder, 7234. It's P 07234.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. Prosecutor. Before we move on to the next document, we're still talking about document P 764 -- 7064. Amongst other things, the witness proposed that teams of the military prosecutor's office be formed, if I understood him well. Can I please ask the witness: Where from should have these teams have arrived, from Croatia, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, or from some other area, bearing in mind the fact that the witness has stated that he was not subordinated to anybody from the republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is true. I was not subordinated to anybody from the Republic of Croatia, as the Presiding Judge has just said. In item 2 of my proposal to Mr. Susak, I meant the officials from the military prosecutor's office and the military courts in the Republic of Croatia. I assumed that in these institutions there might be people who had been born in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I wanted them to come and help with the -- with the establishment of the military prosecutor's office and military courts in the Croatian Defence Council, i.e., in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, please turn to document 7234, P 07234. Can you tell us, sir, what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: 7234. I apologise, is that the document you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this will document is, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: This is the second letter to Mr. Gojko Susak, who at the time was the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the purpose -- what was the purpose behind you sending this document to Minister Susak on the 18th of December, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: The reason was that I considered him influential in the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and I believe that he could help with resolving some issues that I was aware of at the time in the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, "I believe that he could help with resolving some issues," what kind of help do you believe that he could render?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: By using his influence and help I meant people and materiel assistance in the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you turn, sir, to the subsection of this document dealing with the Tomislavgrad ZP, please.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you look, please, at the fifth paragraph of that document, which in the English says: "Staffing policy is wrong. Some are favoured and extolled for no reason." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the second paragraph on the last page, page 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's a different page number in the English translation, but let me see. It's the sentence, sir, that says in English: "Staffing policy is wrong."

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: It's the second paragraph, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, on the last page. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Well, it says: "Staffing policy is wrong. Some are favoured and extolled for no reason." Well, I think that that is a sentence which speaks of the fact that in -- among certain cadres in the Croatian Defence Council there are different opinions than is evident by the results. And I can't really say who this referred to specifically speaking because the sentence is a general one. It's a generalised observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, my last question before the next break: At the end of the next paragraph there is a reference to appointing -- appointing yes-men to responsible positions. Do you see that, and can you perhaps explain what that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Which paragraph did you say? Some help here, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's the very next paragraph after the sentence concerning staffing policy, at the end of that paragraph. The third sentence of the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: In that paragraph I proposed that the protagonists of assignments should be clearly defined, and the civilian authorities must make their contribution and not view this from the sidelines, and that they are in -- responsible for the situation because they tied HVO units to themselves. And as far as I was informed, part of the Presidency appointed people who would be yes-men and respond to them, not to the hierarchy and chain of command up towards the Main Staff. So that's how I used this word "yes-men."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. We are -- the translation, I'm told, is not correct, or it's -- it's off a little bit when it refers to Presidency, because I think he's referring to local municipalities, and I think this is very clear, because he makes it eminently clear in his statement and his reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you to clarify that, sir, because you were -- there were two things that you said and I would like you to elaborate upon them. This point is when -- this reference to "Presidency", if you could explain what -- the Presidency at what level. And the second one is you make reference to "the civilian authorities," and that's on line 6 of page 67. Can you please explain what you meant by "the civilian authorities" and also explain the level of the Presidency with respect to the government structure?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I didn't use the word "Presidency." I said representatives of civilian authorities at the level of municipalities, because the brigades of the Croatian Defence Council were organised at the time on a municipal level and were financed mostly from the municipal budget. So I mean the representatives of the Croatian Defence Council in the civilian authority bodies at the level of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I note the time, Mr. President. This is perhaps a good spot for the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 25 to 6.00. We're taking a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, we're now going to turn to the topic of collection centres and centres for prisoners of war, and just so that we're all clear, can you tell us what facility or facilities you are referring to when you use the phrase "collection centre"?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: When I use the word "collection centres," I mean collection centres --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the -- could the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the knowledge I had so far, the collection centres of Gabela were mentioned, followed by Heliodrom, the military investigation prison of Ljubuski, and later on when we implemented the decision of the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, I learnt of the existence of the collection centre at Rama or, rather, Prozor. And then there was, under the authority of the Ministry of the Interior in Livno and Tomislavgrad, two others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever hear of a facility at Dretelj and, if so, how would you characterise that facility?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: As far as that facility is concerned, I heard about it over the information media in the summer of 1993. I cannot say what kind of collection centre it was. And last time you showed me a film about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: However, upon my arrival it wasn't used as a collection centre, the Dretelj collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And a couple of times earlier today you've used the phrase or we've seen in documents "centres for prisoners of war." What facility or facilities would fall under the description, centres for prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: In the documentation that we mentioned a moment ago there are different titles for the collection centres. Then we have the centre for prisoners of war and the military investigating prison. Now, I don't know the exact titles and names, but as far as I remember from the documents the collection centre existed in Gabela, and in between a collection centre and a centre for prisoners of war at Heliodrom and the military investigation prison was in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about the term, sir, "detention centre"? Did you ever use that term and, if so, to describe what facility or facilities?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Well, I think all these names were used without any decision as to what meant what. Later on when the restructuring and reorganising took place, we determined what a centre for prisoners of war was, but at that time I wasn't able to determine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Biskic, at the time that you arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 8th of November, 1993, were you aware that there were any rules or regulations governing the prisoner of war centres on the territory controlled by the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Upon arrival, since I wasn't in charge of that kind of thing, I didn't have the documents, but later on when I became aware of the situation and got to know about these matters I had documents which were signed by Mr. Bruno Stojic as the head of the defence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you please turn, sir, to document P 01474, or in your bundle it should be 1474. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am. That's the document I referred to a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection, this document was in force at the time you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Nobody put it -- I do believe it was in force. It didn't go out of force, and I think it was in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, approximately the first time you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I can't say that, but I think it was November and December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, why you saw this document or the reason why you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, but probably when we were discussing the detention centres or collection centres somebody showed me the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what your reaction, if any, was when you reviewed this document or saw this document for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Biskic, when you sought more information about the collection centres or prisoner of war centres?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I said that I issued an order to the acting deputy on the 17th of November. I think that's when the document was issued. And I asked a report -- for a report and information about the situation in the collection centres, and I think that I asked some 13 or 14 questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And upon issuing this order seeking information, what response, if any, did you receive?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I received a report from the acting head of the military police, Mr. Lavric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn, please, to the document marked 6695. That is P 06695. Can you tell us, Mr. Biskic, what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: This document says "An analysis of the capacities for accommodation," et cetera, et cetera. It says, "Head of the military police administration," and it is addressed to me. It isn't signed. You showed me the document last time, and I said I wasn't sure whether I saw it during that period of time, and I say the same thing here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With respect, sir, to the information contained in this document, did you at any point in time have reason to determine whether this information is accurate or inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: When this document came about, the date of it, I didn't establish whether it was accurate or not. However, later on when the decision was implemented by the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, his decision, we received exact data about the situation in the collection centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell me a little bit or tell us a little bit about the exact data about the situation you received concerning the collection centres?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, do you mean as far as the document that I have in my hands is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, you just told us at lines 5 through 8 on page 72, "Later on when the decision was implemented by the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, we received exact data about the situation in the collection is centres," and so my question at this point is: Do you recall what that exact data that you received concerned, or what that exact data was?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I think that pursuant to the report by the service for exchange of detainees and others on the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, in the decision we received a summarised report, and as far as I remember, the figure was 3 -- 4.320, and I think in the report it says what the exact number was per collection centre, or centre for prisoners of war, or prisons, as is the term used here. You showed me that report last time, and it will be able to provide you with concrete figures more specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's turn now, sir, to 6805. That's P 06805. Mr. Biskic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: It's rather an illegible document, but I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell -- can you tell us what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: It's a document whereby the acting head of the military police administration, Mr. Lavric, is responding to an order from me and the questions raised with respect to the collection centres or prisons or centres for POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, if you were satisfied with the answers that you received from Mr. Lavric?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say whether I was satisfied or not. I believe that Mr. Lavric provided responses and answers which were the only ones he could have given at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what do you base that conclusion on, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I base that conclusion on the fact that everybody that's signing a document probably stands by what he wrote. And as far as I knew Mr. Lavric, the general feeling was that he was an honourable officer and did not avail himself of untruths.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Biskic, as a result of this initial information that you received in November 1993, what steps, if any, did you take with respect to the collection centres or centres for prisoners of war on the territory of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already mentioned that once the first information was received I informed Minister Jukic; and the chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council, General Roso. The result of that report was that General Roso issued an order disallowing any detainees to be taken out and saying that they should be returned. And Mr. Jukic issued an order or gave a task to the assistant minister for the sector of health telling him to establish a team of physicians to visit all the collection centres or, rather, the places where detainees were being hold held to see what the situation was like, how they were accommodated and fed and so on, and to propose measures to the minister for improving the conditions. At the same time, I proposed that these problems that were noted should be resolved, and this I did at the meetings held in the Main Staff and the Ministry of Defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please turn, sir, to document 7075. It's P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I interject? A very simple question. Mr. Biskic, did you personally visit any detention centres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. After they were dismantled, it was only sometime in December or the second half of December that I visited Heliodrom, but in the period of time to which this document refers my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, can you please turn to P 07075 or 7075 in your binder. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: This document is the result of an order from the minister of defence, Mr. Jukic, on the reorganisation of the military police. And I said at the time that the military police company for providing security to the centre for POWs was being established, and by this document I as the assistant minister to the acting head of the military police administration give instructions for certain activities linked to the military police company, to establish that company, and among other things, I state that until the formation establishment of the company is resolved and the officers appointed and named I instruct that the acting head of security be Mr. Stanko Bozic, who was the warden up until that time at Heliodrom, and that I subordinate to him the commander of the platoon in the Ljubuski prison, and I regulate other issues for the work of that company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, there's a sentence towards the bottom of this document that's underlined that refers to taking of prisoners for labour. Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you put this sentence in this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Before that I said that we had a lot about certain informations and that prisoners were taken for work. I also said that the chief of the Main Staff had issued an order on a ban to take prisoners away and on return of those who had previously been taken away. Since a company was being set up in order to provide security for the an accommodation of prisoners and which was part system of the military police, and in that way they were subordinated to me through the chief of the administration, I believe that no prisoners could be taken away for work without the approval of the security sector that I was the head of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When did you first become aware, Mr. Biskic, that prisoners were being taken for labour?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly when this was, but it was in November. Soon after that, the chief of the Main Staff issued an order about the ban on such practices. I believe that it was in mid-November, or at least this is when I received information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Biskic, this reference to the security sector, can you tell the Trial Chamber what the security sector was and who was in charge of the security sector?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: In the concept of organisation of the Ministry of Defence, the new concept, there was a security sector or the sector for security issues, and the administration of military police was part of that sector as well as the security services administration. As of the 1st December, I became the assistant minister, and as such I was also the head of the security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Biskic, in response to a question from Judge Trechsel a few moments ago, you told us that you visited Heliodrom. Do you recall when that was that you went to Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was in mid-December or during the implementation of the decision on the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. I can't recall the date but this was sometime between the 15th and 20th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recall what you observed when you went to Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: At the time only those who could be treated as prisoners were taken to Heliodrom. Prisoners, prisoners of war, or persons against whom criminal charges were filed for rebellion. You know that at the beginning of the Serbian aggression against the territory inhabited by Muslims and Croats and during the first stages of the defence, this defence was organised jointly by Croats and Muslims, and some of the Muslims were members of the -- the HVO until the beginning of their mutual conflict, as you may well know. And those and as well as those who were arrested in combat remained in Heliodrom, and the rest were either in the detention centre in Gabela or had already left for the third countries or had been released into the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna or had left to the territories under the control of the Muslim armed forces or the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In other words, the decision was being under implementation and the other collection centres were being dismantled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, at the time you -- at the time you visited Heliodrom, what types of persons were being detained there?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I said that they were detained if criminal charges were raised or could have been raised against them, those who could be treated as prisoners of war. And I believe, at the time, Mr. Bozic told me that from Prozor and Rama he received a few minors and women. And after that I wrote a letter to the president of the commission for exchanges asking him to take those persons over and transport them to Gabela. And I believe that I stated that the numbers were higher than they should have been. I inspected the outpatients' clinic, and I insisted on further measures and actions that would lead to the improved conditions of life and accommodation of these people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware, sir, that any persons who might be described as mentally handicapped were being detained in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, last time you showed me a letter in which this is stated for a fact, and then I said I didn't know whether such individuals had entered the collection centre or whether the consequences that they suffered were the result of their stay in the collection centre. I said that I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Do you recall issuing an oral order to Mr. Bozic concerning such persons?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I think that something was said to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please look at the next document in the binder, 7209, which is P 07209. Do you see the reference, sir, to an oral order from yourself on this document signed by Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that this was during my visit to the prisoner of war accommodation on the 16th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn, please, sir, to the next document, 7266, P 07266. Do you recognise this document, Mr. Biskic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document refers to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: The document refers to sending the report that was sent to me by the chief of the security services administration, and it contains what they observed while prisoners were being released from Heliodrom and Gabela.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn now, sir, to the next document in the binder, 7269, P 07269? And again, Mr. Biskic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what this document relates to, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: The document relates to the instruction on the treatment of prisoners of war. I signed it, and I sent it to the administration of the military police, to the administration of the SIS, to the military prosecutor's office in Mostar, to the military prosecutor's office in Livno, to the military court in Mostar, to the military court in Livno, to the office for the exchanges of detained, to the Red Cross office in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and for the attention of the minister of defence, Mr. Perica Jukic, and assistant minister of health.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Biskic, do you recall what prompted you to issue these instructions on 20 December 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what it was, but I believe that all the circumstances surrounding the collection centres prompted me to do that. As of that moment, the military police took over the control over the detainees, and I believe that it was necessary because of them and because of all of the others involved to issue a -- an instruction on the treatment of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you perhaps elaborate, sir, on the first part of your answer when you said, "I believe that all the circumstances surrounding the collection centres," prompted you to do that? What do you mean by "all the circumstances surrounding the collection centres"?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: It was from the previous documents that when I say circumstances it was not clearly defined, which you can also see from the report of the acting head of the security administration who it was who provided security for the prisoners, who authorised the entry into the centres. It was not clear who was in charge and who was -- who had the authority of the lives and well-being of these people. And also in my conversation with the head of the information services, the prisoners of war were not interviewed as they should have been, and that's why yet once again I wanted to issue this instruction to inform everybody again how they should treat prisoners of war from the moment they are detained from -- to the moment when they are finally accommodated in the prisoner of war centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, when you indicate that the prisoners of war were not interviewed as they should have been, what is the consequence of that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I don't know what to say to this. Maybe we did not have the accurate information about what is going on, on the other side, because obviously those were detained in action were best informed about what was going on in -- on the other side, and this is what both the commanders and members of the intelligence always do. They question the detainees who were captured in combat. A prisoner of war, of course, does not have to say anything according to the Geneva Conventions, and it is well known what they are supposed to say and that they shouldn't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What steps or procedures were in place in December 1993 to make determinations as to whether persons being detained were in fact prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I don't know what procedure you're talking about. I'm very clear on the concept of prisoners of war. I did not see a procedure in place save for the instruction that we had just discussed that was signed by Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, for the Judges' information, when it comes to the authorities, could you tell us from your point of view who should have been detained in a military prison? Which individuals could have been detained in a military prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to tell you what the Geneva Conventions prescribe and what is typical of any armed force. In a prisoner of war centre, all those who are treated as prisoners of war, according to the Geneva Conventions, can be detained. Members of the Croatian Defence Council or any members of any other army that have committed crimes or are being processed for a crime they have committed, there are military prisons where you can keep soldiers who have breached discipline, and there can also be collection centres where you put inhabitants of a certain area to protect them, for their own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again I'm told the translation is a little off, Your Honour. Perhaps, I'm told, if the gentleman speaks a little slower they may get a fuller translation, and I think this is rather important, because from his statement he's very clear on what the treatment should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Try to speak slower. What I am interested in is the last term in your response. You said people who inhabit an area, to protect them. Can you please explain? Can you elaborate on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it is a well-known thing everywhere in the world that during a war and in an area where safety is impaired that a certain number of people are moved from the area for their own protection. This is what I meant when I spoke about that last category. You asked me a general question, and I provided you with a reply in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This category, that is "moved for their own protection," what regime of accommodation do they receive? Under what regime of accommodation are they placed, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their accommodation has to be outside of the zone of combat activities, and that accommodation should not be under the authority of the Ministry of Defence or, rather, the armed forces. It has to be under the authority of some civilian institutions, the Red Cross or some other. And again I repeat I'm talking in general terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if we have a situation in which a civilian from Mostar finds him or herself in Heliodrom, in your view, what is that person's situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very hard to answer this, this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me try one more question in this respect, sir. What procedures or steps were in place to ensure that civilians who were being kept for their own protection were not commingled with prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I have answered in general terms. I have not spoken about any specific situation. I believe that there is a procedure for that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what that procedure is?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Where? I apologise. I'm not clear on your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On the territory under the control of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I don't know what procedure was in place. I did not dwell upon that. I deal -- dealt with the -- finding solutions to the situation that I found on the ground when I was involved in all that. But at the moment when the military police under my authority took over the security of the prisoners, then I thought that I should issue an instruction outlining the entire procedure as to how a person can be taken into the prisoners of war centre, how they should be kept there, and this is exactly what the instruction is about, the one that you have just shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, earlier this afternoon, Mr. Biskic, you made reference to closing -- the process of closing the detention centres. Do you recall when that process began?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: At the time when I arrived down there, and I believe that even before that you mentioned Dretelj, when I arrived there Dretelj no longer existed. However, we started working pursuant to the decision of the president of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna that I didn't see, but it did exist. I believe that it was issued on the 10th December, 1993. This was a decision by the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Our activities started on the 11th December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, "Our activities started on the 11th of December," what did you start doing on the 11th of December, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I am talking about implementation of the decision issued on the 10th of December by the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the decision concerning the closing down of the collection centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Biskic, what did you do to begin implementing the order of the 10th of December, 1993, by the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to an invitation to a meeting by Mr. Jukic, we held a meeting on the 11th of November. I believe that that was the date. It was on the 11th of December, 1993, and we agreed methods and ways how we should implement that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall some of the issues that were discussed at this meeting on 11 December 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: I believe that the goal was to set up teams that would simply say which individuals should stay on in the future prisoner of war centres, who are the prisoners that could stay in the area of the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, which persons can go to a third country, and which persons wished to go to the territories under the authority of the Muslim forces, i.e., the forces of the army of BiH. And also, we had to define such institutions which could help us implement all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you please turn, Mr. Biskic, to document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I've been listening very carefully to what you've been saying, and I have perused all the documents signed by you. One question. When you took up your position, did you have any relationship with the judiciary, and particularly with the military prosecutor? Did you meet with any of them? Did you speak to them about the prisoners of war, the procedures, the situation in certain places where people were detained without any charges being raised against them? Did you talk about that to a military prosecutor at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dear President, thank you for your promotion. I'm not a general. I used to be a brigadier and not a general. My contacts with the military prosecutor and military judiciary started in December at the meeting that I've just mentioned, the meeting that took place on the 11th of December. We did not talk about any criminal charges and why they were not raised against certain individuals. We concluded at that meeting that if the criminal charges were not raised, and there were grounds to raise them, that in cooperation with the military prosecutor's office, the military police, and the civilian police, that this should be done in order for us to have the grounds to keep somebody in detention in the prisoner of war centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you well, you are a former officer who was educated in the JNA. You know all the rules, all the regulations. You understand about the military prosecutor's office, the military courts and prisoners of war, and you know that one cannot be detained if there's no decision of a military court or a military judge. Did you know all that or did you not know this? Did you not know about this rule?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the former officer of the former army, of course I am familiar with the Geneva Conventions and the international humanitarian law, and I know very well who can enjoy the status of a prisoner of war and who cannot. And also, as an officer of the armed forces of the Croatian army and at my arrival in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we applied the same rules in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, can you please turn to document 7148, P 07148. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: This is the record made at this meeting which was held on the 11th of December, 1993. At this meeting we discussed the ways to implement the decision of the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna on dismantling all the collection centres in the territory of the Croatian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina [as interpreted]. I emphasise this is a record. This is not a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Biskic, you chaired this meeting on this day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall reviewing these minutes after the meeting in December 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether there were anything reported in these minutes that were incorrect or inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe anything was recorded that was inaccurate, although I'm sure that not everything that was discussed was entered into the minutes, because the minutes are not the same as stenographic notes. But of course the key issues are contained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, there's reference in this -- in these minutes to some information conveyed by Mr. Berislav Pusic concerning the location of detention centres in HR HB. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Berislav Pusic was present at the meeting, and he took the floor at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember what he said about the detention centres on the territory of the HR HB and where they were located?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see from these minutes, the first thing that Mr. Berislav Pusic said was about the situation in Livno 71 where -- and Tomislavgrad 42 and Gabela 1.256. I assume that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, if you look above that, sir, it says after Colonel Biskic's opening remark Mr. Berislav Pusic took the floor. This is about four paragraphs above what you were just referring to. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And there's reference to detention centres operating in Capljina, Gabela, Mostar, Heliodrom, Tomislavgrad, Livno, Prozor, Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Before what Mr. Pusic said, I think that it's when he took the floor first, he says where the detention centres existed, and I think that coincides with later reports on the dismantling of these centres. Sujica is probably the Tomislavgrad area, because Sujica is in the vicinity of Tomislavgrad, but I can't claim that there wasn't a centre in Sujica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Biskic, according to the list of attendees at the top of these minutes, it would appear that Mr. Goran Dodig, the assistant to the Republic of Croatia minister of defence, was present. Do you recall if Mr. Dodig was in fact present?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Goran Dodig was present at the meeting. I don't know in what capacity though. I don't believe he was assistant to the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia. I don't think he appeared in that capacity, but otherwise he's a physician and was born in the area of Herzegovina, but I don't his exact role.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you don't -- just to be clear, you don't know his capacity or role. You don't know why Mr. Dodig attended the meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know in what capacity he was there and who assigned him to the meeting or invited him to the meeting, because I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you turn, sir, to the next document, 7194, P 07194. Do you see this document, sir, 7194?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This reference in the first paragraph of the document to the killing of a prisoner in the Gabela detention centre, can you elaborate upon that, or can you provide any further information on that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: All I can say is what it says here attached to this document or letter that I sent to the acting head of the military police department. And I think this event is one that Mr. Previsic mentioned at a meeting of the 11th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps in light of that answer Mr. Biskic if you can return to the previous document, which was P 07148, and I believe it's on page 4 of the Croatian version of the document, and it's page 8 in the English translation. Do you recall Mr. Previsic, at this meeting on the 11th of December, 1993, talking about an incident involving a detainee in Gabela?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN BISKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Judging from these minutes, Mrs. Boko -- Mr. Boko Previsic, was indeed present at the meeting, as were the warden of Ljubuski and Gabela and Heliodrom. And in the minutes on page 4, if that is correct, and I do believe it is, Mr. Previsic informed those present that he had to protect himself because a prisoner had attacked him and that he was killed.
